claim: Using ribosome profiling, both a global translational repression and approximately 200 mRNAs that undergo specific translational regulation at mitotic entry were identified.
source: Here, using ribosome profiling, we find both a global translational repression and identified ∼200 mRNAs that undergo specific translational regulation at mitotic entry.
evidence: The claim is supported by ribosome profiling data presented in the manuscript, which is an experimental technique used to measure translation.

claim: Few changes in mRNA abundance are observed during mitosis, indicating that regulation of translation is the primary mechanism of modulating protein expression during mitosis.
source: In contrast, few changes in mRNA abundance are observed, indicating that regulation of translation is the primary mechanism of modulating protein expression during mitosis.
evidence: This claim is based on RNA-seq data comparing mRNA levels across cell cycle phases, combined with inference about the primary regulatory mechanism.

claim: 91% of the mRNAs that undergo gene-specific regulation in mitosis are translationally repressed, rather than activated.
source: Interestingly, 91% of the mRNAs that undergo gene-specific regulation in mitosis are translationally repressed, rather than activated.
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the ribosome profiling data analysis.

claim: Emi1 is one of the most pronounced translationally-repressed genes during mitosis.
source: One of the most pronounced translationally-repressed genes is Emi1, an inhibitor of the anaphase promoting complex (APC) which is degraded during mitosis.
evidence: This is based on ribosome profiling data showing strong translational repression of Emi1.

claim: Emi1 is an inhibitor of the anaphase promoting complex (APC).
source: One of the most pronounced translationally-repressed genes is Emi1, an inhibitor of the anaphase promoting complex (APC) which is degraded during mitosis.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about Emi1's function.

claim: Emi1 is degraded during mitosis.
source: One of the most pronounced translationally-repressed genes is Emi1, an inhibitor of the anaphase promoting complex (APC) which is degraded during mitosis.
evidence: This is established knowledge about Emi1 regulation, also confirmed by data in the manuscript.

claim: Full APC activation requires translational repression of Emi1 in addition to its degradation.
source: We show that full APC activation requires translational repression of Emi1 in addition to its degradation.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing APC substrate degradation in cells with and without Emi1 translational repression.

claim: Gene-specific translational repression is a means of controlling the mitotic proteome that may complement post-translational mechanisms for inactivating protein function.
source: These results identify gene-specific translational repression as a means of controlling the mitotic proteome, which may complement post-translational mechanisms for inactivating protein function.
evidence: This is an interpretation and speculation based on the Emi1 data and broader findings.

claim: Changes in the abundance of hundreds of proteins occur during the cell cycle.
source: Genome-wide microarray, RNA sequencing (RNA-seq), and protein-based mass spectrometry studies have revealed changes in the abundance of hundreds of proteins during the cell cycle (Cho et al., 2001; Whitfield et al., 2002; Aviner et al., 2013; Grant et al., 2013; Lane et al., 2013; Stumpf et al., 2013; Ly et al., 2014), many of which are specifically expressed in G2 phase and mitosis (G2/M).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Many proteins are specifically expressed in G2 phase and mitosis.
source: Genome-wide microarray, RNA sequencing (RNA-seq), and protein-based mass spectrometry studies have revealed changes in the abundance of hundreds of proteins during the cell cycle (Cho et al., 2001; Whitfield et al., 2002; Aviner et al., 2013; Grant et al., 2013; Lane et al., 2013; Stumpf et al., 2013; Ly et al., 2014), many of which are specifically expressed in G2 phase and mitosis (G2/M).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Transcriptional regulation plays an important role in cell cycle-stage specific protein expression patterns.
source: Transcriptional regulation plays an important role in this temporal expression pattern, as many genes show cell cycle-stage specific expression of their mRNA level (Cho et al., 2001; Whitfield et al., 2002).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Many genes show cell cycle-stage specific expression of their mRNA level.
source: Transcriptional regulation plays an important role in this temporal expression pattern, as many genes show cell cycle-stage specific expression of their mRNA level (Cho et al., 2001; Whitfield et al., 2002).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Regulated protein degradation plays a key role in sculpting the proteome during the cell cycle.
source: Regulated protein degradation also plays a key role in sculpting the proteome during the cell cycle, particularly at the end of mitosis when a large set of proteins is ubiquitinated by the E3 ubiquitin ligase, the Anaphase Promoting Complex (APC), and then degraded by the proteasome (Peters, 2006).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: At the end of mitosis, a large set of proteins is ubiquitinated by the Anaphase Promoting Complex (APC) and then degraded by the proteasome.
source: Regulated protein degradation also plays a key role in sculpting the proteome during the cell cycle, particularly at the end of mitosis when a large set of proteins is ubiquitinated by the E3 ubiquitin ligase, the Anaphase Promoting Complex (APC), and then degraded by the proteasome (Peters, 2006).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: Changes in translation efficiency can modify protein abundance during the cell cycle.
source: In addition to regulation of transcription and protein degradation, changes in translation efficiency (TE) also can modify protein abundance during the cell cycle.
evidence: This is general knowledge about gene regulation mechanisms.

claim: Translational regulation plays a particularly important role during the specialized cell division cycles of meiosis and early embryonic development.
source: Translational regulation plays a particularly important role during the specialized cell division cycles of meiosis and early embryonic development, since transcription is largely silent at this stage (Mendez and Richter, 2001; Groisman et al., 2002; Tadros and Lipshitz, 2009; Weill et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Transcription is largely silent during meiosis and early embryonic development.
source: Translational regulation plays a particularly important role during the specialized cell division cycles of meiosis and early embryonic development, since transcription is largely silent at this stage (Mendez and Richter, 2001; Groisman et al., 2002; Tadros and Lipshitz, 2009; Weill et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Lengthening of poly(A) tails through polyadenylation results in translational activation in vertebrate oocyte meiosis.
source: For example, initial work on meiosis in vertebrate oocytes revealed that lengthening of the poly(A) tails of dormant mRNAs through polyadenylation results in translational activation, which plays a critical role in meiotic progression (Weill et al., 2012; Subtelny et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Translational activation through polyadenylation plays a critical role in meiotic progression.
source: For example, initial work on meiosis in vertebrate oocytes revealed that lengthening of the poly(A) tails of dormant mRNAs through polyadenylation results in translational activation, which plays a critical role in meiotic progression (Weill et al., 2012; Subtelny et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Translational regulation has been described in somatic cells.
source: While somatic cells appear to use transcriptional regulation as a major mechanism for modulating protein expression during the cell cycle, translational regulation has been described in somatic cells as well (Sivan and Elroy-Stein, 2008; Novoa et al., 2010; Kronja and Orr-Weaver, 2011; Aviner et al., 2013; Stumpf et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Changes in poly(A) tail length can occur during G2 phase of the mitotic cell cycle.
source: As in meiosis, changes in the poly(A) tail length can occur during G2 phase of the mitotic cell cycle (Novoa et al., 2010), but these effects appear to be less important for translational regulation during the somatic cell cycle than during early embryonic development (Subtelny et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Poly(A) tail length changes appear to be less important for translational regulation during the somatic cell cycle than during early embryonic development.
source: As in meiosis, changes in the poly(A) tail length can occur during G2 phase of the mitotic cell cycle (Novoa et al., 2010), but these effects appear to be less important for translational regulation during the somatic cell cycle than during early embryonic development (Subtelny et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: Translation is thought to be globally repressed during mitosis.
source: Perhaps the most striking example of translation regulation in the somatic cell cycle occurs during mitosis, when translation is thought to be globally repressed (Fan and Penman, 1970).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: Global translational repression during mitosis appears to be sequence-independent and likely affects most mRNAs.
source: This global translational repression appears to be sequence-independent, and likely affects most mRNAs (Fan and Penman, 1970).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: The functional significance of global translational repression during mitosis remains unknown.
source: While such global translational repression was observed many decades ago, its functional significance remains unknown.
evidence: This is a statement about the state of knowledge in the field.

claim: Global translational repression may facilitate the selective synthesis of proteins that can escape global inhibition through IRES-dependent translation.
source: Several studies suggested that this global translational repression may facilitate the selective synthesis of a small number of proteins that can escape global inhibition through a non-canonical, mRNA cap-independent translation initiation mechanism dependent on internal ribosome entry sites (IRESes) (Cornelis et al., 2000; Pyronnet et al., 2000; Qin and Sarnow, 2004; Schepens et al., 2007; Wilker et al., 2007; Marash et al., 2008; Ramirez-Valle et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Recent work challenged the view that translation in mitosis is mediated to a significant extent by IRESes.
source: However, recent work challenged the view that translation in mitosis is mediated to a significant extent by IRESes, and instead found that canonical, cap-dependent translation dominates in mitosis (Shuda et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: Canonical, cap-dependent translation dominates in mitosis.
source: However, recent work challenged the view that translation in mitosis is mediated to a significant extent by IRESes, and instead found that canonical, cap-dependent translation dominates in mitosis (Shuda et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: Ribosomal profiling uses deep sequencing of ribosome-protected mRNA fragments to quantify ribosome occupancy on individual mRNAs.
source: The recent development of ribosomal profiling, a method that uses deep sequencing of ribosome-protected mRNA fragments to quantify ribosome occupancy on individual mRNAs, allows the TE of single mRNA species to be examined at a system-wide level (Ingolia et al., 2009, 2011).
evidence: This is a description of the ribosome profiling method, supported by citations.

claim: A recent study found hundreds of genes that show changes in translation efficiency during the cell cycle.
source: A recent study applied this technology to investigate the mechanism of cell cycle-dependent translational control and found hundreds of genes that show changes in TE during the cell cycle (Stumpf et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: Many mRNAs showed altered translation rates in mitosis when compared to either G1 or S phase cells in a previous study.
source: Many mRNAs showed altered translation rates in mitosis when compared to either G1 or S phase cells.
evidence: This refers to findings from a previous study (Stumpf et al., 2013).

claim: A previous study did not include analysis of G2 phase cells, which is required to determine whether observed changes are mitosis-specific.
source: However, this study did not include analysis of G2 phase cells, which is required to determine whether observed changes are mitosis-specific, as G2 phase cells are very similar to mitotic cells, but very different from G1- or S-phase cells, at least with respect to mRNA levels (Cho et al., 2001; Whitfield et al., 2002).
evidence: This is a critique of a previous study based on knowledge about cell cycle phases.

claim: G2 phase cells are very similar to mitotic cells, but very different from G1- or S-phase cells, at least with respect to mRNA levels.
source: However, this study did not include analysis of G2 phase cells, which is required to determine whether observed changes are mitosis-specific, as G2 phase cells are very similar to mitotic cells, but very different from G1- or S-phase cells, at least with respect to mRNA levels (Cho et al., 2001; Whitfield et al., 2002).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Previous studies of mitotic translational regulation relied on synchronizing cells in mitosis with microtubule targeting drugs.
source: Previous studies of mitotic translational regulation relied on synchronizing cells in mitosis with microtubule targeting drugs (Fan and Penman, 1970; Pyronnet et al., 2001; Stumpf et al., 2013), but recent work has shown that translation rates are dramatically affected by treatment with such drugs (Sivan et al., 2011; Coldwell et al., 2013), thereby complicating the annotation of mitosis-specific translation effects.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Translation rates are dramatically affected by treatment with microtubule targeting drugs.
source: Previous studies of mitotic translational regulation relied on synchronizing cells in mitosis with microtubule targeting drugs (Fan and Penman, 1970; Pyronnet et al., 2001; Stumpf et al., 2013), but recent work has shown that translation rates are dramatically affected by treatment with such drugs (Sivan et al., 2011; Coldwell et al., 2013), thereby complicating the annotation of mitosis-specific translation effects.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: A modest (~35%) global translational repression of the bulk of mRNAs occurs during mitosis in RPE-1 cells.
source: First, using metabolic labeling of non-transformed RPE-1 cells, we find a modest (∼35%) global translational repression of the bulk of mRNAs during mitosis, which is consistent with findings in other studies (Fan and Penman, 1970; Bonneau and Sonenberg, 1987; Pyronnet et al., 2001).
evidence: This is based on metabolic labeling data from the current study and is consistent with previous studies.

claim: A subset of approximately 200 mRNAs show much larger (>threefold) gene-specific changes in their translation efficiency during mitosis.
source: In addition to this modest global repression, using ribosomal profiling, we identify a subset ∼200 of mRNAs that show much larger (>threefold), gene-specific changes in their TE during mitosis.
evidence: This is based on ribosome profiling data from the current study.

claim: The large majority of the ~200 translationally-regulated mRNAs are repressed at mitotic entry and then translationally re-activated at mitotic exit.
source: The large majority of the latter group of mRNAs are translationally repressed at mitotic entry and then translationally re-activated at mitotic exit, highlighting the precise temporal specificity of this gene-specific translational regulation.
evidence: This is based on ribosome profiling data comparing different cell cycle phases.

claim: Translational repression, rather than IRES-dependent activation of mRNA translation, is the dominant method of gene-specific translational regulation in mitosis.
source: Thus, translational repression, rather than IRES-dependent activation of mRNA translation, is the dominant method of gene-specific translational regulation in mitosis, although minor effects of IRES-dependent translation cannot be ruled out.
evidence: This is an inference based on the ribosome profiling data showing predominantly repression.

claim: Translational repression of Emi1 in mitosis is important to prevent new Emi1 protein synthesis at a time when the existing Emi1 protein pool is degraded.
source: Follow-up studies on one of these translationally repressed genes, Early mitotic inhibitor 1 (Emi1), a potent inhibitor of the APC, reveals that translational repression in mitosis is important to prevent new Emi1 protein synthesis at a time when the existing Emi1 protein pool is degraded.
evidence: This is based on experimental data showing effects of Emi1 translational regulation on APC activity.

claim: The combined activities of protein degradation and translational repression ensures the complete removal of Emi1 protein, which enhances APC activation and the degradation of APC substrates at the end of mitosis.
source: These results lead to a model in which the combined activities of protein degradation and translational repression ensures the complete removal of Emi1 protein, which enhances APC activation and the degradation of APC substrates at the end of mitosis.
evidence: This is a model based on experimental data and inference.

claim: Translational regulation can enhance the efficiency of post-translational protein inhibition.
source: These results provide the first genome-wide view of the translational changes that occur specifically in mitosis and reveal that translational regulation can enhance the efficiency of post-translational protein inhibition, which may represent a more general function for translational repression.
evidence: This is an inference and speculation based on the Emi1 data.

claim: RPE-1 cells were synchronized in late G2, mitosis, or early G1 using the CDK1 inhibitor RO-3306.
source: We synchronized RPE-1 cells in late G2 (G2), mitosis (M) or early G1 (G1) with a specific small molecule CDK1 inhibitor, RO-3306, using a previously established synchronization protocol (Vassilev et al., 2006) (Figure 1A).
evidence: This describes the experimental method used, supported by a citation.

claim: CDK1 is largely inactive during G2 and only becomes activated at the end of G2/prophase.
source: CDK1 is largely inactive during G2 and only becomes activated at the end of G2/prophase (Jackman et al., 2003; Gavet and Pines, 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The CDK1 inhibitor prevents the progression out of G2, but the low CDK1 state in the presence of the inhibitor reflects the normal G2 phase in unsynchronized cells.
source: Thus, the inhibitor prevents the progression out of G2, but the low CDK1 state in the presence of the CDK1 inhibitor reflects the normal G2 phase in unsynchronized cells (Jackman et al., 2003; Gavet and Pines, 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies and describes the rationale for the synchronization method.

claim: Pure (95%) populations of M and G1 cells can be obtained based upon the timing of release from G2 arrest.
source: To release cells from G2, the CDK1 inhibitor is washed out and the cells progress into M and then G1, and pure (95%) populations of M and G1 cells can be obtained based upon the timing of release from G2 arrest (Figure 1B,C).
evidence: This is supported by FACS and microscopy data shown in Figure 1B,C.

claim: The cell synchronization protocol using RO-3306 is minimally perturbing and avoids the use of drugs that arrest cells in mitosis by targeting microtubules.
source: Thus, this cell synchronization protocol is minimally perturbing and avoids the use of drugs that arrest cells in mitosis by targeting microtubules, which are known to affect translation (Sivan et al., 2011; Coldwell et al., 2013).
evidence: This is a characterization of the method with citations supporting the concern about microtubule drugs.

claim: Using S35-methionine labeling, a global decrease in mRNA translation during mitosis was found when compared to G2 and G1 cells.
source: Using S35-methionine labeling, we found a global decrease in mRNA translation during mitosis when compared to G2 and G1 cells respectively (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is based on metabolic labeling data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: The magnitude of global translational repression in mitosis is smaller (~35% reduction) than previously reported (70% reduction).
source: This finding confirms the global reduction in translation during mitosis reported by other studies (Fan and Penman, 1970; Bonneau and Sonenberg, 1987; Pyronnet et al., 2001); however, the magnitude of the effect seen here is smaller (∼35% reduction in our study vs 70% found previously [Fan and Penman, 1970]).
evidence: This compares current data with previous studies.

claim: The difference in magnitude of global translational repression might be due to the use of microtubule inhibitors in previous studies.
source: This difference might be due to the use of microtubule inhibitors in cells arrested in mitosis in previous studies, which can cause global translational repression (Sivan et al., 2011; Coldwell et al., 2013).
evidence: This is speculation based on known effects of microtubule inhibitors.

claim: Only 25 genes were down-regulated in M compared to G2 (>threefold), and not a single gene was up-regulated.
source: Comparing mRNA abundance in G2 vs M cells, we detected only 25 genes that were down-regulated in M and not a single up-regulated gene (>threefold, see 'Materials and methods' section) (Figure 2A, red bars, left graph).
evidence: This is based on RNA-seq data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: When G2 cells were compared to G1 cells, 220 genes were down-regulated and 82 genes were up-regulated in G1.
source: In contrast, when G2 cells were compared to G1 cells, 220 genes were down-regulated and 82 genes up-regulated in G1 (Figure 2A, red bars, middle graph).
evidence: This is based on RNA-seq data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: When M cells were compared to G1 cells, 138 genes were up-regulated and 156 genes were down-regulated in M.
source: Similarly, when M cells were compared to G1 cells, many mRNAs were changed (138 up and 156 down in M) (Figure 2A, red bars, right graph).
evidence: This is based on RNA-seq data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: The mRNAs that changed between G1 and G2 were mostly the same set that also changed between G1 and M.
source: The mRNAs that changed between G1 and G2 were mostly the same set that also changed between G1 and M (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A); 96% of mRNAs that are up-regulated in G1 vs G2 are also increased at least twofold in G1 vs M.
evidence: This is based on RNA-seq data analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A.

claim: 80% of mRNAs that are down-regulated in G1 vs G2 are also decreased at least twofold in G1 vs M.
source: Similarly, 80% of mRNAs that are down-regulated in G1 vs G2, are also decreased at least twofold in G1 vs M.
evidence: This is based on RNA-seq data analysis.

claim: The mRNA content of G2 and M phase cells is very similar, but distinct from G1 phase cells.
source: Together, these results indicate that the mRNA content of G2 and M phase cells is very similar, but distinct from G1 phase cells.
evidence: This is an inference based on the RNA-seq data.

claim: The vast majority of gene-specific changes in translation efficiency were observed when M phase transcripts were compared with either G2 or G1.
source: The vast majority of gene-specific changes in TE were observed when M phase transcripts were compared with either G2 or G1; 199 and 92 genes were translationally regulated between M and either G2 or G1, respectively.
evidence: This is based on ribosome profiling data analysis.

claim: Only 13 genes showed changes in translation between G2 and G1.
source: In contrast, only 13 genes showed changes in translation between G2 and G1 (Figure 2A, blue bars; transcripts with >threefold difference in TE, and >twofold difference in ribosome footprint (FP) density were scored as translationally controlled, see 'Materials and methods' for more details).
evidence: This is based on ribosome profiling data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Translation efficiency is similar in G2 and G1, but very different in M.
source: Thus, in contrast to mRNA abundance, which is similar in G2 and M, but distinct in G1, TE is similar in G2 and G1, but very different in M.
evidence: This is an inference based on the ribosome profiling and RNA-seq data.

claim: The mRNA levels of the 199 genes that showed gene-specific translational regulation in M were largely constant throughout the cell cycle.
source: When we analyzed mRNA abundance of the 199 genes that showed gene-specific regulation in M, we found that their mRNA levels were largely constant throughout the cell cycle (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is based on RNA-seq data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: The translation efficiency of genes known to be transcriptionally regulated was largely constant.
source: Similarly, the TE of genes known to be transcriptionally regulated was largely constant (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is based on ribosome profiling data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Gene-specific translational regulation affects a different set of genes than transcriptional regulation.
source: These results indicate that gene-specific translational regulation affects a different set of genes than transcriptional regulation.
evidence: This is an inference based on the comparison of translationally and transcriptionally regulated genes.

claim: Of the 199 mRNAs that show gene-specific translational regulation in M compared to G2, 182 were translationally downregulated in M and only 17 were upregulated.
source: The vast majority of the 199 mRNAs that show gene-specific translational regulation in M compared to G2 were repressed rather than activated; comparing M to G2, 182 were translationally downregulated in M and only 17 were upregulated (Figure 2A, blue bars, middle graph; Figure 2—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is based on ribosome profiling data shown in Figure 2A and Figure 2—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Of the 92 mRNAs that were translationally regulated between M and G1, 86 were repressed in M, and only 6 were activated.
source: Similarly, of the 92 mRNAs that translationally regulated between M and G1, 86 were repressed in M, and only 6 were activated (Figure 2A, blue bars, right graph; Figure 2—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is based on ribosome profiling data shown in Figure 2A and Figure 2—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Of the 182 genes that were translationally repressed in M compared to G2, 87% were repressed >twofold in M compared to G1.
source: The genes that were translationally repressed in M vs G2 were mostly also repressed in M vs G1; of the 182 genes that were repressed in M compared to G1, 87% were repressed >twofold in M compared to G1.
evidence: This is based on ribosome profiling data analysis.

claim: There is a good correlation in the fold change in translation efficiency between G2 vs M and G1 vs M for individual mRNAs.
source: Furthermore, there is a good correlation in the fold change in TE between G2 vs M and G1 vs M for individual mRNAs (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is based on ribosome profiling data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: When cells progress from G2 to M, gene-specific translational regulation is dominated by repression, and the genes that are translationally repressed as cells enter mitosis are mostly re-activated upon mitotic exit.
source: In summary, when cells progress from G2 to M, gene-specific translational regulation is dominated by repression, and the genes that are translationally repressed as cells enter mitosis are mostly re-activated upon mitotic exit.
evidence: This is a summary inference based on the ribosome profiling data.

claim: Many genes that exhibited variations in mRNA levels during the cell cycle are involved in cell division.
source: Many genes that exhibited variations in mRNA levels during the cell cycle are involved in cell division (p-values < 10−9, see 'Materials and methods').
evidence: This is based on gene ontology enrichment analysis of RNA-seq data.

claim: The translationally regulated genes included many signaling molecules, transcription factors, and transmembrane proteins.
source: In contrast, the translationally regulated genes were functionally very different from the transcriptionally regulated genes and included many signaling molecules, transcription factors, and transmembrane proteins (significantly enriched with p-values < 10−8) (see Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is based on gene ontology enrichment analysis of ribosome profiling data.

claim: Multiple components of the PI3 kinase pathway were translationally repressed during mitosis.
source: For example, multiple components of the PI3 kinase pathway were translationally repressed during mitosis (Figure 2—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This is based on ribosome profiling data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2A.

claim: The mitotic phosphatases PP1γ and PP2aβ showed mitosis-specific translational downregulation.
source: We also found mitosis-specific translational downregulation of the mitotic phosphatases PP1γ and PP2aβ (Figure 2—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: This is based on ribosome profiling data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2B.

claim: During mitosis, PP1γ and PP2aβ phosphatases are strongly inhibited through phosphorylation and binding to inhibitory proteins.
source: During mitosis, these phosphatases are strongly inhibited through phosphorylation and binding to inhibitory proteins (Wurzenberger and Gerlich, 2011), suggesting that mitotic translational repression may represent an additional back-up mechanism to inhibit protein function (see Discussion).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: Overexpression of either PP1γ or PP2aβ phosphatase strongly disrupted normal cell division.
source: Consistent with this notion, we found that overexpression of either PP1γ or PP2aβ phosphatase strongly disrupted normal cell division (Figure 2—figure supplement 3A–C).
evidence: This is based on time-lapse microscopy data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3A–C.

claim: Two key regulators of centriole duplication, Plk4 and CP110, showed strong translational repression.
source: We also found a strong translational repression of two key regulators of centriole duplication, Plk4 and CP110 (Figure 2—figure supplement 2C) (Chen et al., 2002; Habedanck et al., 2005).
evidence: This is based on ribosome profiling data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2C, with citations supporting their role in centriole duplication.

claim: The majority of histones showed a strong reduction in protein synthesis in M compared with G2.
source: Finally, the majority of histones showed a strong reduction in protein synthesis in M compared with G2.
evidence: This is based on ribosome profiling data.

claim: Transcriptional and gene-specific translational control dominate at different stages of the cell cycle.
source: Taken together, these results show that transcriptional and gene-specific translational control dominate at different stages of the cell cycle (transcription at the G1-to-G2 transition and translational regulation dominating at the more rapid G2-to-M transition) and regulate a distinct set of genes.
evidence: This is an inference based on the combined RNA-seq and ribosome profiling data.

claim: A fluorescence-based reporter was developed to analyze translation of individual transcripts in living cells.
source: To validate the results obtained in our ribosome profiling experiments in living cells, we developed a fluorescence-based reporter to analyze translation of individual transcripts in living cells.
evidence: This describes the development of a new experimental tool.

claim: The fluorescence reporter consists of a GFP fused to an inducible degron, which is continuously degraded until a small molecule stabilizer is added.
source: In brief, the reporter consists of a GFP fused to an inducible degron, which is continuously degraded until a small molecule stabilizer is added (Iwamoto et al., 2010) (Figure 3A).
evidence: This describes the reporter design with a citation and reference to Figure 3A.

claim: Upon addition of the stabilizer drug, time-lapse microscopy revealed an increase in the GFP/mCherry ratio over time, which reflects the translation rate of the GFP.
source: Upon addition of the stabilizer drug, time-lapse microscopy revealed an increase in the GFP/mCherry ratio over time, which reflects the translation rate of the GFP (Figure 3B,C, see 'Materials and methods').
evidence: This is based on time-lapse microscopy data shown in Figure 3B,C.

claim: Transcripts with UTRs from translationally repressed mRNAs showed decreased synthesis in mitosis compared with interphase.
source: While the UTRs of control transcripts did not lead to translational regulated of the GFP reporter, time-lapse imaging revealed that the transcripts with UTRs from translationally repressed mRNAs showed decreased synthesis in mitosis compared with interphase (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is based on time-lapse microscopy data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: The results from the fluorescence reporter provide strong, independent validation of the ribosome profiling dataset.
source: These results provide strong, independent validation of the ribosome profiling dataset and show that regulatory elements present in 5′ and 3′ UTRs confer translational repression in mitosis.
evidence: This is an inference based on the agreement between ribosome profiling and reporter data.

claim: Regulatory elements present in 5′ and 3′ UTRs confer translational repression in mitosis.
source: These results provide strong, independent validation of the ribosome profiling dataset and show that regulatory elements present in 5′ and 3′ UTRs confer translational repression in mitosis.
evidence: This is based on the fluorescence reporter data showing UTR-dependent regulation.

claim: Emi1 mRNA was present at similar levels in G2 and M as determined by single molecule FISH.
source: To establish that mRNA levels of Emi1 remain unchanged as cells progress into mitosis, we performed single molecule FISH and found that Emi1 mRNA was present at similar levels in G2 and M (Figure 3—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: This is based on single molecule FISH data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1E.

claim: The translational repression of Emi1 was conferred by the 3′UTR of Emi1 alone.
source: Furthermore, we mapped the regulatory element in the Emi1 UTRs, and found that the translational repression was conferred by the 3′UTR of Emi1 alone, which is identical in all Emi1 mRNA isoforms (Figure 3—figure supplement 1D,F).
evidence: This is based on fluorescence reporter data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1D,F.

claim: All 5′UTR isoforms of Emi1 in combination with the Emi1 3′UTR were regulated in a similar manner.
source: Consistent with this, all 5′UTR isoforms in combination with the Emi1 3′UTR were regulated in a similar manner (Figure 3—figure supplement 1D,F).
evidence: This is based on fluorescence reporter data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1D,F.

claim: The 3′UTR of Emi1 is sufficient for translational regulation during mitosis.
source: Together, these results confirm the conclusion that the inhibition of Emi1 protein synthesis in M is due to translational repression, and show that the 3′UTR of Emi1 is sufficient for this translational regulation.
evidence: This is an inference based on the UTR mapping data.

claim: In G2 phase, Emi1 inhibits APC/Cdh1, and this inhibition is required to allow accumulation of cyclins in G2 and for mitotic entry.
source: In G2 phase, Emi1 inhibits APC/Cdh1, and this inhibition is required to allow accumulation of cyclins in G2 and for mitotic entry (Reimann et al., 2001; Hsu et al., 2002; Di Fiore and Pines, 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: In early mitosis, Emi1 protein is inactivated both through protein degradation and CDK1-dependent phosphorylation.
source: However, in early mitosis, Emi1 protein is inactivated both through protein degradation and CDK1-dependent phosphorylation (Reimann et al., 2001; Guardavaccaro et al., 2003; Margottin-Goguet et al., 2003; Moshe et al., 2011), which is likely required for APC/Cdh1 activation and APC substrate degradation in the subsequent telophase/G1.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: mCherry-Emi1 was degraded in late G2/early mitosis.
source: First, we confirmed that mCherry-Emi1 was degraded in late G2/early mitosis (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A), as found previously (Guardavaccaro et al., 2003; Margottin-Goguet et al., 2003).
evidence: This is based on time-lapse microscopy data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A, consistent with previous studies.

claim: Aurora A, Plk1, and CDC20 are APC/Cdh1 substrates.
source: As a readout of APC/Cdh1 activity, we expressed fluorescently-tagged Aurora A, Plk1 or CDC20, all of which are APC/Cdh1 substrates. (Peters, 2006).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: Fluorescence reporter substrates Aurora A, Plk1, and CDC20 were all rapidly degraded in anaphase/telophase in control cells.
source: These fluorescence reporter substrates were all rapidly degraded in anaphase/telophase in control cells as expected (Figure 4A–C).
evidence: This is based on time-lapse microscopy data shown in Figure 4A–C.

claim: When Emi1 lacking its normal translation regulatory elements was expressed, APC/Cdh1 activation in telophase was partially inhibited.
source: When Emi1 lacking its normal 5′ and 3″ translation regulatory elements was expressed, cells progressed through mitosis normally and the bulk of Emi1 protein was degraded; however, APC/Cdh1 activation in telophase was partially inhibited, as indicated by the decreased degradation of APC/Cdh1 substrates (Figure 4A–C and Video 1).
evidence: This is based on time-lapse microscopy data shown in Figure 4A–C and Video 1.

claim: Exogenous Emi1 was expressed at similar levels as the endogenous gene.
source: Importantly, exogenous Emi1 was expressed at similar levels as the endogenous gene in these experiments, as determined by transcript counting by single molecule FISH (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is based on single molecule FISH data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Emi1 protein degradation is insufficient to completely inhibit Emi1 activity in the presence of continued Emi1 synthesis.
source: These results show that Emi1 can inhibit APC/Cdh1 activation at the end of mitosis and suggest that Emi1 protein degradation is insufficient to completely inhibit Emi1 activity in the presence of continued Emi1 synthesis.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental data showing partial APC inhibition.

claim: Translational repression of Emi1 allowed a substantially higher degree of APC/Cdh1 activation at comparable Emi1 expression levels.
source: Strikingly, translational repression of Emi1 in mitosis allowed a substantially higher degree of APC/Cdh1 activation at comparable Emi1 expression levels (Figure 4D,E and Figure 4—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is based on time-lapse microscopy data shown in Figure 4D,E and Figure 4—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Mitosis-specific translational repression of mCherry-Emi1 by ARHGAP5 UTRs allowed APC activation at the end of mitosis to a similar extent as Emi1 UTRs.
source: Indeed, mitosis-specific translational repression of mCherry-Emi1 by ARHGAP5 UTRs allowed APC activation at the end of mitosis to a similar extent as Emi1 UTRs (Figure 4D,E).
evidence: This is based on time-lapse microscopy data shown in Figure 4D,E.

claim: Examination of Emi1 mRNA localization during mitosis did not reveal localization to a specific site in the cell.
source: Furthermore, examination of Emi1 mRNA localization during mitosis did not reveal localization to a specific site in the cell (Figure 4—figure supplement 1D), arguing against a role for the UTRs of Emi1 in mRNA localization, but rather indicating that their primary function is to repress translation during mitosis.
evidence: This is based on single molecule FISH data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1D.

claim: Emi1 was more completely depleted when protein degradation was combined with translational repression.
source: Interestingly, Emi1 was more completely depleted when protein degradation was combined with translational repression (Figure 4F).
evidence: This is based on time-lapse microscopy data shown in Figure 4F.

claim: Inactivation of existing Emi1 protein through degradation and potentially inhibitory phosphorylation is insufficient to completely inhibit Emi1 activity.
source: These results demonstrate that inactivation of existing Emi1 protein, through degradation and potentially inhibitory phosphorylation (Moshe et al., 2011), is insufficient to completely inhibit Emi1 activity, but when post-translational inactivation is combined with translational repression, Emi1 is more thoroughly inhibited, which allows robust APC activation.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental data, with a citation supporting phosphorylation.

claim: When post-translational inactivation is combined with translational repression, Emi1 is more thoroughly inhibited, which allows robust APC activation.
source: These results demonstrate that inactivation of existing Emi1 protein, through degradation and potentially inhibitory phosphorylation (Moshe et al., 2011), is insufficient to completely inhibit Emi1 activity, but when post-translational inactivation is combined with translational repression, Emi1 is more thoroughly inhibited, which allows robust APC activation.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental data.

claim: The mitotic translational program is dominated by a modest global translational repression, combined with potent repression of a subset of mRNAs.
source: Thus in summary, the mitotic translational program is dominated by a modest global translational repression, combined with potent repression of a subset of mRNAs, which acts on top of the global repression.
evidence: This is a summary inference based on all the translational data.

claim: Translational repression of Emi1 acts as a mechanism to enhance post-translational protein inactivation.
source: Our follow-up studies on Emi1 suggests that its translational repression acts as a mechanism to enhance post-translational protein inactivation, which could represent a more general function of translational repression in mitosis and in other processes.
evidence: This is an inference and speculation based on the Emi1 data.

claim: The evidence for mitosis-specific translational repression of specific mRNAs is supported by ribosomal profiling and a fluorescence reporter assay.
source: The evidence for mitosis-specific translational repression of specific mRNAs is supported by two separate methodologies. The first evidence comes from ribosomal profiling which measures ribosome occupancy of native transcripts, but does not provide a direct measure of translation itself. The second method involves the use of an introduced (thus non-native) reporter mRNA that provides a real-time, live-cell readout of protein production from translation.
evidence: This describes the two methodologies used to support the claims.

claim: In test cases where both ribosome profiling and fluorescence reporter methods were applied, good agreement in the results was found.
source: In the test cases where both methods were applied, we find good agreement in the results, providing strong support for widespread gene-specific translational repression in mitosis.
evidence: This is based on comparison of results from both methods.

claim: The genome-wide comparison of translation efficiency of G1 vs M cells yields very similar results to the comparison of G2 vs M cells.
source: First, the genome-wide comparison of TE of G1 vs M cells (neither of which have any drug present) yields very similar results to the comparison of G2 (RO-3306 present) vs M cells.
evidence: This is based on ribosome profiling data comparing different cell cycle phases.

claim: The CDK1 inhibitor is only present in the G2 sample, a time at which CDK1 is mostly inactive in unperturbed cells.
source: Third, the CDK1 inhibitor is only present in our G2 sample, a time at which CDK1 is mostly inactive in unperturbed cells (Jackman et al., 2003; Gavet and Pines, 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The translation inhibitor 4E-BP1, which is phosphorylated by CDK1 in mitosis, is not detectably phosphorylated in G2.
source: Consistent with this, the translation inhibitor 4E-BP1, which is phosphorylated by CDK1 in mitosis, is not detectably phosphorylated in G2 (Heesom et al., 2001).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: The synchronized G2 sample closely mimics the G2 phase of unsynchronized cells with respect to CDK1 activity.
source: Thus, our synchronized G2 sample closely mimics the G2 phase of unsynchronized cells with respect to CDK1 activity.
evidence: This is an inference based on the CDK1 activity data and synchronization method.

claim: The sets of genes that show altered translation efficiency and mRNA abundance are largely non-overlapping.
source: Interestingly, the sets of genes that show altered TE and mRNA abundance (likely due, at least in part, to transcriptional regulation) are largely non-overlapping (Figure 2B,C).
evidence: This is based on comparison of RNA-seq and ribosome profiling data shown in Figure 2B,C.

claim: The cell cycle timing of transcriptional and translational regulation differ; the majority of gene-specific translational changes occur at entry and exit from mitosis, while transcriptional changes predominate between G1 and G2.
source: Furthermore, the cell cycle timing of transcriptional and translational regulation also differ; the majority of gene-specific translational changes occur at entry and exit from mitosis (G2-to-M and M-to-G1 transitions), while transcriptional changes predominate between G1 and G2.
evidence: This is an inference based on the RNA-seq and ribosome profiling data.

claim: The dominant function of gene-specific translational regulation during mitosis is to potently inhibit synthesis of a relatively small subset of the proteome.
source: Thus, we conclude that the dominant function of gene-specific translational regulation during mitosis is to potently inhibit synthesis of a relatively small subset of the proteome.
evidence: This is an inference based on the ribosome profiling data showing predominantly repression.

claim: The distinct use of transcriptional and translational regulatory mechanisms is consistent with the timing of the cell cycle transitions for which they are used.
source: The distinct use of transcriptional and translational regulatory mechanisms is consistent with the timing of the cell cycle transitions for which they are used; regulating transcription is a relatively slow mechanism for altering protein synthesis rates, because of the time required for transcription, mRNA processing/nuclear export and mRNA turnover.
evidence: This is an inference based on knowledge of gene regulation mechanisms and cell cycle timing.

claim: Regulating transcription is a relatively slow mechanism for altering protein synthesis rates.
source: The distinct use of transcriptional and translational regulatory mechanisms is consistent with the timing of the cell cycle transitions for which they are used; regulating transcription is a relatively slow mechanism for altering protein synthesis rates, because of the time required for transcription, mRNA processing/nuclear export and mRNA turnover.
evidence: This is based on knowledge of gene regulation mechanisms.

claim: Translational control alters protein synthesis rates almost instantaneously.
source: On the other hand, translational control alters protein synthesis rates almost instantaneously, which makes it well suited to the short time scale of mitosis, which is generally less than 1 hr in most somatic cells with doubling times of 1–2 days.
evidence: This is based on knowledge of translational regulation and cell cycle timing.

claim: Mitosis is generally less than 1 hour in most somatic cells with doubling times of 1–2 days.
source: On the other hand, translational control alters protein synthesis rates almost instantaneously, which makes it well suited to the short time scale of mitosis, which is generally less than 1 hr in most somatic cells with doubling times of 1–2 days.
evidence: This is general knowledge about cell cycle timing.

claim: A recent study of mouse dendritic cell activation found that the vast majority of changes in protein synthesis were due to altered mRNA abundance, rather than due to changes in translation rates.
source: Interestingly, a recent study of mouse dendritic cell activation, which happens at a time-scale of many hours, similar to the G1-S transition, found that the vast majority of changes in protein synthesis were due to altered mRNA abundance, rather than due to changes in translation rates (Jovanovic et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: Translational control is rapidly reversible, enabling protein synthesis to restart quickly when cells exit from mitosis and enter G1.
source: A second unique feature of translational control is its rapid reversibility, enabling protein synthesis to restart quickly when cells exit from mitosis and enter G1.
evidence: This is based on knowledge of translational regulation mechanisms.

claim: Translational control may be employed when acute changes in protein synthesis are needed, while transcriptional control is used to affect slower changes in gene expression.
source: Thus, translational control may be employed when acute changes in protein synthesis are needed (e.g., entry into and exit from mitosis), while transcriptional control is used to affect slower changes in gene expression.
evidence: This is an inference based on the data and knowledge of gene regulation mechanisms.

claim: Very few mRNAs showed substantial (>threefold), gene-specific translational activation during mitosis.
source: A surprising finding of this study is that very few mRNAs showed substantial (>threefold), gene-specific translational activation during mitosis.
evidence: This is based on ribosome profiling data.

claim: In previous reported cases of translational regulation of specific mRNAs during mitosis, the findings were predominantly of translational activation through an IRES-dependent mechanism.
source: In previous reported cases of translational regulation of specific mRNAs during mitosis, the findings were predominantly of translational activation through an IRES-dependent mechanism (Cornelis et al., 2000; Pyronnet et al., 2000; Qin and Sarnow, 2004; Wilker et al., 2007; Marash et al., 2008; Ramirez-Valle et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: A small number of mRNAs (16 and 6) were translationally upregulated >threefold in mitosis compared to G2 and G1, respectively.
source: While we also found a small number of mRNAs that were translated more efficiently during mitosis (16 and 6 mRNAs were translationally upregulated >threefold in mitosis compared to G2 and G1, respectively), the vast majority of regulated mRNAs were translationally repressed (187 and 97 mRNAs were downregulated in mitosis compared to G2 and G1, respectively).
evidence: This is based on ribosome profiling data.

claim: The vast majority of regulated mRNAs were translationally repressed (187 and 97 mRNAs were downregulated in mitosis compared to G2 and G1, respectively).
source: While we also found a small number of mRNAs that were translated more efficiently during mitosis (16 and 6 mRNAs were translationally upregulated >threefold in mitosis compared to G2 and G1, respectively), the vast majority of regulated mRNAs were translationally repressed (187 and 97 mRNAs were downregulated in mitosis compared to G2 and G1, respectively).
evidence: This is based on ribosome profiling data.

claim: IRES-mediated upregulation of translation in mitosis may be relatively weak compared to the threefold cut-off used to identify changes in gene-specific translation efficiency.
source: One possible explanation for this discrepancy is that the IRES-mediated upregulation of translation in mitosis may be relatively weak compared to the cut-off (>threefold) that we have used in this study to identify changes in gene-specific TE.
evidence: This is speculation about why few IRES-dependent genes were found.

claim: A previous study of IRES-mediated translational upregulation found that only one of three proteins examined was upregulated by > threefold.
source: A previous study of IRES-mediated translational upregulation found that only one of three proteins examined was upregulated by > threefold (Qin and Sarnow, 2004).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: A recent study found that translation in mitosis is dominantly cap-dependent.
source: Furthermore, a recent study found that translation in mitosis is dominantly cap-dependent (Shuda et al., 2015), suggesting that IRES-mediated translation may only make a minor contribution to the translational landscape in mitosis.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: IRES-mediated translation may only make a minor contribution to the translational landscape in mitosis.
source: Furthermore, a recent study found that translation in mitosis is dominantly cap-dependent (Shuda et al., 2015), suggesting that IRES-mediated translation may only make a minor contribution to the translational landscape in mitosis.
evidence: This is an inference based on a citation to a previous study.

claim: The dominant function of gene-specific translational regulation is to shut down rather than activate synthesis of proteins during mitosis.
source: The results from our work and Shuda et al., while not ruling out IRES-dependent translational activation of some genes in mitosis, indicates that the dominant function of gene-specific translational regulation is to shut down rather than activate synthesis of proteins during mitosis.
evidence: This is an inference based on the current data and a previous study.

claim: Oocytes stockpile maternal mRNA, as new transcription does not occur until the mid-blastula stage of development.
source: Oocytes stockpile maternal mRNA, as new transcription does not occur until the mid-blastula stage of development.
evidence: This is general knowledge about oocyte biology.

claim: In oocytes, translational regulation is the main mechanism by which protein synthesis rates are tuned due to the absence of transcriptional control.
source: Due to the absence of transcriptional control, translational regulation is the main mechanism by which protein synthesis rates are tuned.
evidence: This is general knowledge about oocyte biology.

claim: In oocytes, translational regulation occurs largely by modulating poly(A) tail length.
source: In these systems, translational regulation occurs largely by modulating poly(A) tail length (Weill et al., 2012; Subtelny et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Regulation of poly(A) tail length does not appear to be a general mechanism for controlling translation efficiency in somatic cells.
source: While changes in poly(A) tail length also occur on a subset of mRNAs during the mitotic cell cycle (Novoa et al., 2010), regulation of poly(A) tail length does not appear to be a general mechanism for controlling TE in somatic cells (Subtelny et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Translational control in meiosis is most likely mechanistically distinct from the gene-specific translational regulation during mitosis.
source: Thus, translational control in meiosis is most likely mechanistically distinct from the gene-specific translational regulation during mitosis described here.
evidence: This is an inference based on the differences in mechanisms.

claim: In meiosis, regulatory mechanisms mainly function to specifically activate a subset of mRNAs.
source: Consistent with this, we find that the large majority of regulated mRNAs are translationally repressed during mitosis, while in meiosis regulatory mechanisms mainly function to specifically activate a subset of mRNAs (Mendez and Richter, 2001).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: The sets of genes that are regulated during meiosis and mitosis are largely non-overlapping.
source: Furthermore, the sets of genes that are regulated during meiosis and mitosis are largely non-overlapping.
evidence: This is based on comparison of the current data with knowledge of meiotic regulation.

claim: Emi1 is translationally regulated during both meiosis and mitosis.
source: Interestingly, Emi1 is an exception to this rule, as it is translationally regulated during both meiosis (Belloc and Mendez, 2008) and mitosis (this study).
evidence: This is based on the current data and a citation to a previous study.

claim: In meiosis, Emi1 is translationally activated through control of its poly(A) tail length by the RNA binding protein CPEB.
source: However, in meiosis it is translationally activated through control of its poly(A) tail length by the RNA binding protein CPEB (Belloc and Mendez, 2008).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: Mutation of all CPEB binding sites in the 3′UTR of Emi1 does not prevent translational repression in mitosis.
source: This does not appear to be the case during mitosis, as mutation of all CPEB binding sites in the 3′UTR of Emi1 does not prevent translational repression in mitosis (unpublished observation).
evidence: This is based on unpublished experimental data.

claim: The gene-specific translational control program in mitosis is distinct from the meiotic translation program.
source: Therefore, we conclude that the gene-specific translational control program in mitosis identified here is distinct from the meiotic translation program.
evidence: This is an inference based on the mechanistic differences.

claim: The average protein half-life is many hours.
source: The average protein half-life is many hours (Schwanhausser et al., 2011), while mitosis takes less than an hour, so inhibition of protein synthesis for this short period of time is not expected to have a major impact on overall protein levels.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: Inhibition of protein synthesis during mitosis is not expected to have a major impact on overall protein levels.
source: The average protein half-life is many hours (Schwanhausser et al., 2011), while mitosis takes less than an hour, so inhibition of protein synthesis for this short period of time is not expected to have a major impact on overall protein levels.
evidence: This is an inference based on protein half-life and mitosis duration.

claim: In the presence of continued protein synthesis, degradation cannot remove all of the Emi1, resulting in a small amount of residual Emi1 protein levels at the end of mitosis.
source: However, we find that in the presence of continued protein synthesis, degradation cannot remove all of the Emi1, resulting in a small amount of residual Emi1 protein levels at the end of mitosis, which can interfere with full APC activation.
evidence: This is based on experimental data showing Emi1 levels and APC activity.

claim: When new Emi1 protein synthesis is inhibited through translational repression, Emi1 is eliminated more completely.
source: In contrast, when new Emi1 protein synthesis is inhibited through translational repression, Emi1 is eliminated more completely (Figure 5).
evidence: This is based on experimental data shown in Figure 5.

claim: Transcriptional inhibition at the G2/M transition would not afford a similar effect to translational repression, since protein synthesis rates would not decline substantially within the required time-scale due to relatively slow mRNA turnover.
source: Transcriptional inhibition at the G2/M transition would not afford a similar effect, since protein synthesis rates would not decline substantially within the required time-scale due to relatively slow mRNA turnover.
evidence: This is an inference based on knowledge of mRNA turnover rates.

claim: Of the proteins that are translationally repressed at the G2-to-M transition, very few are known to be degraded during mitosis.
source: However, of the proteins that are translationally repressed at the G2-to-M transition, very few are known to be degraded during mitosis, leaving open the question of why they are translationally repressed.
evidence: This is based on knowledge of protein degradation during mitosis.

claim: Translationally repressed proteins may be inactivated during mitosis through other post-translational mechanisms, such as phosphorylation.
source: One possibility is that these proteins are inactivated during mitosis through other post-translational mechanisms, such as phosphorylation.
evidence: This is speculation about the function of translational repression.

claim: Newly synthesized proteins are unphosphorylated and thus active, so inhibition of translation will limit the formation of such new, active protein and thus enhance post-translational protein inactivation.
source: As newly synthesized proteins are unphosphorylated and thus active, inhibition of translation will limit the formation of such new, active protein and thus enhance post-translational protein inactivation.
evidence: This is an inference based on knowledge of protein phosphorylation.
